Mary Shelley. The English author and author of Frankenstein, often considered the first science fiction novel. Born into a family of radical intellectuals, she synthesized gothic sensibilities with scientific speculation, creating a work that explored the ethics of creation and the consequences of unchecked ambition. Her imaginative depth extended to other speculative works that shaped the contours of fantastic literature. Shelley wrote Frankenstein at age eighteen, published in 1818, presenting a rationalized monster-making narrative that grounded the fantastic in plausible science—a turning point for speculative fiction. She conceived the work during the famous 1816 ghost-story contest at Villa Diodati with her husband Percy Bysshe Shelley, Lord Byron, and others. Shelley authored The Last Man in 1826, an apocalyptic novel set in the twenty-first century that pioneered plague narrative and end-times speculation. She was the daughter of philosopher William Godwin and feminist writer Mary Wollstonecraft, inheriting a tradition of challenging conventional thought. Shelley wrote numerous works of short fiction, essays, and the autobiographical novel Lodore, exploring themes of isolation and social constraint. Her works emphasize the isolation of the outsider—whether creator or created—and the cost of transgressing natural and social boundaries, establishing her legacy as foundational to science fiction itself.
